We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.

title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
summary: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) enforce such requirements with a semidefinite program that minimally modifies a nominal control input. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.

title: DS and AMDS Symbol-Pair Codes from Three Families of Simple Root Cyclic Codes
summary: Symbol-pair distances of simple-root cyclic codes are important for evaluating error correction performance under overlapping pair read channels. In this paper, we construct three families of simple-root cyclic codes over finite fields of odd characteristic via generator polynomials. For length \(2q+2\), the minimum symbol-pair distance is \(10\) for every odd prime power \(q\ge 7\), established by excluding invalid support configurations. For length \(4q-4\), when \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\) and finite field constraints hold, it is \(9\) or \(10\). For length \(2(q-1)\), reciprocal-polynomial analysis shows it is \(11\) or \(12\). All obtained codes are MDS or AMDS symbol-pair codes.

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
summary: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

title: Design Choices for Multimodal Transformer Learning with Missing and Longitudinal Healthcare Data
summary: Multimodal learning offers the potential to improve predictions by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous data sources. However, multimodal datasets are frequently incomplete, raising important questions about how models should handle missing information. Although recent approaches increasingly rely on Transformer-based architectures for multimodal fusion, incomplete multimodal data introduces challenges such as missing modalities and intra-modal missingness, which motivate key architectural design choices, such as tokenization granularity. In addition, many datasets are longitudinal, with observations collected across multiple time points. The sequential nature of the Transformer architectures provides a natural framework for modeling such data, but introduces additional considerations, such as how temporal information should be represented. In this study, we systematically investigate these design choices using three different cancer datasets. We compare modality-level and feature-level tokenization and evaluate attention masking and imputation as strategies for handling missing information, both naturally occurring in the datasets and synthetically induced. We further investigate approaches for incorporating temporal information in our training process and how to model it. Experiments are conducted with unimodal and multimodal configurations, as well as different levels of missingness for binary survival classification and multiple time encoding strategies for discrete-time survival prediction. Our results show that while multimodal outperforms unimodal results, missing data heavily impacts predictions and thus effective design choices such as tokenization granularity, and intra-missing handling is essential for reliable prediction.

title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

title: From Transfer Probes to Expert Grouping: Evidence from LoRA Post-Training
comment: Technical report for training resources allocation for specialization of LLMs
summary: A platform that post-trains one base model for many business lines often has more lines than experts it can maintain, so lines must share experts, yet lines seldom come with a taxonomy saying which should share. We ask whether transfer probes (train on one source, measure paired changes on all sources) can discover a grouping when the standard one is unknown. To test probes against a reference, we use seven public sources that do have a label tree (five mathematics subfields and two kinds of programming, standing in for business lines) and treat the tree's grouping as a label reference that the evaluator holds and the method does not. With four LoRA experts under fixed per-source exposure and per-expert budgets, we compare a purely probe-derived grouping and an uninformed uniform default (whose tied routing serves every line from one expert) against this reference. Trained once for one interval from a shared warm-up state and routed by a rule fixed by each allocation, neither reached the prespecified practical gain of 2 percentage points, and both had lower overall utility than the reference ($-2.43$ and $-2.54$ pp; 95\% intervals below zero). In a post hoc comparison, the probe-derived grouping was indistinguishable from the uniform default ($+0.11$ pp, $[-1.25,+1.54]$). In fixed-budget LoRA post-training, a grouping built from initial-state single-source probes thus did not deliver the advantage predicted from the probes once carried to a later training state, a finite budget, and specified routing.

title: Compositional Sensitivity Analysis for Multiobjective System Co-Design
summary: Sensitivity analysis of coupled systems typically propagates derivatives of single-valued maps, whereas multiobjective optimization generally treats sensitivity at the system level rather than through interconnected subsystems. We develop a mathematical framework for compositional sensitivity analysis in multiobjective system design, building on monotone co-design. Subsystems are represented as design problems (DPs), interconnected through series, parallel, union, intersection, and feedback composition. We introduce tangential DPs (TDPs) to describe first-order variations around an operating point, show that they preserve the structure of DPs, and characterize their queries through graphical derivatives. To account for multiple internal realizations of a system-level operating point, tangential co-design problems compose families of local TDPs by taking a union over these realizations while retaining the original interconnection structure. We show that these compositions yield families of TDPs and establish conditions under which sensitivity analysis commutes with individual composition operations. Beyond infinitesimal sensitivity, we show that bounded tangential models of convex DPs provide tighter outer approximations of feasible finite changes, which can be propagated through co-design problems without union compositions. We conclude with several convex and nonconvex numerical examples that showcase the framework's accuracy and computational benefits.

title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
summary: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.

title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026), Hawaii, USA
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.

title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.

title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $ρ$ by $ρ^α$ for a data-adaptive exponent $α\in[0,1]$: $α=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $α=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $α$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $κ$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$α$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.

title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
summary: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.

title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
summary: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.

title: Taylor-Approximation-Based Repair of High Floating-Point Errors
summary:
Numerical libraries can still lose many bits of accuracy on localized ill-conditioned inputs, such as roots, poles, cancellation points, and branch boundaries. This paper presents NPTaylor, a Taylor-approximation-based framework for repairing localized high floating-point errors in numerical C routines. Given a high-error input, a localized repair domain, a high-precision oracle, and an error threshold, NPTaylor searches over Taylor degree, expansion center, segmentation, and floating-point evaluation strategy. It emits guarded C patches that use a generated Taylor evaluator inside the repair domain and fall back to the original routine outside it. Candidate patches are accepted only after validating the emitted C code on recorded local samples, guard endpoints, and the pre-repair peak input. The generated evaluator uses coefficient splitting and compensated Horner evaluation to reduce rounding error introduced by the patch itself.
  We evaluate NPTaylor on GSL benchmark workloads. On 38 one-input functions, both NPTaylor and AutoRNP repair all 114 configurations across three accuracy thresholds. NPTaylor is 3.33x faster by geometric-mean offline repair time and emits 0.162x as many C bytes. In the strictest setting, its median repair time is 3.74s versus 81.97s for AutoRNP. NPTaylor also repairs localized multi-input benchmark cases beyond AutoRNP's implemented one-input workflow. These results show that Taylor-based guarded patches can provide compact, efficient local repairs, while the claims remain validation-relative rather than full-domain proofs.

title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
summary: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

title: Symmetric two-level preconditioning for the method of reflections
summary: We develop and analyze a symmetric two-level preconditioner for the method of reflections for Laplace problems in perforated domains. Using constant boundary modes, we define a coarse correction through a symmetric coercive dual formulation. Combining this coarse correction with parallel reflection corrections gives a symmetric positive definite preconditioner for solving the dual system by the conjugate gradient method. Under a geometric separation condition, we prove a condition number bound independent of the number and sizes of the holes and the diameter of the ambient domain. We also derive geometry-dependent convergence estimates for the one-level methods that explain the need for a coarse correction.

title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
summary: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Project website: https://jevolution.world
summary: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.

title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.

title: Learning to Extrapolate in Depth with Looped Transformers
summary: Looped transformers reuse a single block across iterations, raising a natural question: how far can a block trained at one depth be safely extrapolated to greater depths? We study this question for all-pairs graph connectivity, where harder graphs require longer-range information propagation. We show that under exchangeability and symmetric positive initialization, population training at depth K converges to an update rule governed by a single effective parameter that balances graph propagation against fitting structure unresolved at training depth. This trade-off creates a finite extrapolation window: too few test-time loops provide insufficient propagation, while too many eventually create false connections. We derive explicit endpoints for this window and bound the graph hardness solvable beyond training as a function of training depth and hardness. In particular, a test depth chosen solely from the training distribution can guarantee recovery on substantially harder graphs, with a certified depth gain that grows exponentially as training depth outpaces training hardness. Experiments validate the predicted windows and show how compute budget and initialization affect the optimal training depth.

title: Convergence of Least Squares Methods for PDEs on R^d with Shallow ReLU^k Networks
summary: We establish inverse inequalities in Gaussian Sobolev norms for shallow $\mathrm{ReLU}^k$ trial spaces. The estimates identify the sharp regularity threshold and quantify the dependence on parameter separation and bias magnitude. Based on these estimates, we prove convergence of weighted least squares discretizations of linear PDEs on $\mathbb R^d$ using shallow networks with prescribed inner parameters and finitely many residual samples in an expanding ball. Under suitable stability and regularity assumptions, we obtain an error bound of order $h^{k+(d+1)/2-r}δ_\pm^{-(S-r)}$ in the Gaussian Sobolev norm of order $S$, up to logarithmic factors, where $r$ is the PDE order, $h$ is the parameter fill distance, and $δ_\pm$ is the antipodal separation. The convergence results cover deterministic and random sampling and extend to fixed bounded regions by restriction. We construct parameter sets with $δ_\pm\asymp h$, yielding a convergence rate in terms of the network width that matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and provide practical guidance on balancing accuracy and stability.

title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
summary: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

title: Rethinking SZZ Search Strategies: Lessons from Claude Code
summary: Identifying bug-inducing commits (BICs) is important for studying software bugs and maintaining software, yet the accuracy of existing SZZ methods remains limited. Although various improvements have been proposed, many SZZ methods still rely on code tracing, which searches for BICs by tracing code changed in a bug-fixing commit (BFC) back to earlier commits. However, this approach may miss the actual BIC when the code responsible for introducing a bug differs from the code modified to fix it. To overcome this limitation, we investigate whether BIC identification can be improved by exploring search strategies that are not constrained to start with code tracing. We use Claude Code, a coding agent that has demonstrated high BIC identification accuracy in prior research, to explore such strategies. Rather than prescribing a search process or providing predefined candidate commits, we allow Claude Code to independently investigate a Git repository. We evaluate its identification accuracy and search behavior on 79 Java cases from 70 repositories. In 79.7% of runs, Claude Code reviewed commit histories before inspecting individual code diffs. It used commit messages to select changes for closer inspection. With this approach, Claude Code achieves an F1 score of 0.771, significantly outperforming all ten evaluated SZZ baselines. Our failure analysis also reveals incorrect oracle labels and ambiguities in BIC definitions in the studied evaluation dataset. After reconstructing the evaluation dataset to address these issues, Claude Code achieves an F1 score of 0.938. A key lesson from Claude Code for improving SZZ search strategies is to use semantic information to find relevant commits and then examine their code changes, rather than starting with code tracing.

title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
summary: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
summary: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.

title: Memory-Augmented Phase-Field Modeling: Onsager Formulation, Internal-Variable Lifting, and Structure-Preserving Computation
summary: In this work, we develop a general memory-augmented phase-field (MAPF) framework based on Onsager's variational principle, in which memory effects are incorporated through a general relaxation kernel while preserving the thermodynamic consistency of the underlying system. Rather than treating fractional models as fundamental formulations, we show that they can be interpreted as reduced descriptions associated with specific power-law memory kernels. The proposed MAPF equations provide a unified modeling framework for non-Markovian phase-field dynamics. To facilitate analysis and computation, we further introduce an equivalent internal-variable representation that transforms the original nonlocal-in-time dynamics into an extended Markovian gradient system. This formulation preserves key structural properties, including energy dissipation and mass conservation, and enables the development of efficient structure-preserving numerical schemes. In particular, we construct an energy-stable scalar auxiliary variable approach combined with a fast rank-one implementation that exploits the relaxation-spectrum-induced coupling structure, resulting in a computationally efficient algorithm with reduced storage requirements. The proposed framework establishes a systematic connection between memory-dependent phase-field modeling, internal-variable thermodynamics, and structure-preserving numerical computation. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, stability, and efficiency of the proposed methods for phase-field dynamics with long-time memory effects.

title: When Is a Reconciliation Break Real? A Temporal Correctness Contract for Streaming Financial Reconciliation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables, 2 propositions. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/reconstream (v1.0.2). Software archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23272623
summary: Reconciliation systems decide, continuously, whether money the ledger expected has arrived at the bank. On an asynchronous stream that decision is taken against partial evidence: a credit that has not appeared may be missing, or may simply not have been posted yet. Deployed pipelines settle this with a timeout or a watermark, and the exceptions are treated as findings. We give a temporal correctness contract that says when such a verdict is admissible, relative to a declared per-source lateness bound, and a checker for it that needs no ground truth. The contract separates three things an operator otherwise sees only as a rising break rate: the reconciler decided too early, an input broke the bound it declared, or the money really is gone. On workloads from a published payment simulator, the standard remedy for a stalled streaming join, an idleness timeout, introduces contract violations on 5.42% of obligations (95% CI [3.94, 6.92]) on traffic where the same job without it is exactly sound, and violations vanish once the timeout reaches the slow source's posting period, as predicted. Under a lateness shift, all four identity-based reconcilers we test raise spurious breaks on between 18.3% and 23.0% of the credits the bank did settle, while their contract violation rate stays at or below 1.01%: the checker attributes the loss to 240 bank-side and 413 ledger-side bound violations rather than to the reconcilers. Tracking one horizon per source leaves break latency 12.7% lower on average and halves its tail (p99 224 against 446 ticks) at equal soundness, though it is not cheaper at every cost setting and we report where it loses. An Apache Flink interval join, written the ordinary way, violates the contract on 14.9--20.1% of obligations. The contract is expressible as SQL over the tables a reconciliation system already keeps, agreeing with the reference implementation on all 4,395 verdicts.

title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
summary: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.

title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
summary: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.

title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
summary: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.

title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
summary: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.

title: What Counts as the Same Task? Executable Contracts for Robustness Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents
summary: Robustness tests for tool-using agents often change the agent's environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does. The result tells us about the original task only if the changed test case is still a valid test of that task. Many evaluations decide this with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space. We propose executable task contracts. A contract states which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and it checks each changed test case before the agent runs. We compare validity rules by scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each rule. Across four encoders, embedding thresholds allowed 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, yet rejected 24-45% of valid hostile notes. With a MiniLM cosine threshold, Mistral appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack. Replaying a saved solution and allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways. Evaluations should state, and check, what counts as the same task.

title: Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation
comment: 3 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to IROS 2025 Workshop on Advancements in Aerial Physical Interaction. Best Paper Award Candidate
summary: Omnidirectional aerial robots offer full 6-DoF independent control over position and orientation, making them popular for aerial manipulation. Although there have been advancements in robotic autonomy, human operation remains essential in complex aerial environments. Previously, we proposed an aerial teleoperation system that brings the rotational flexibility of human hands into the unbounded aerial workspace, which was evaluated through a vertically mounted valve-turning task. However, due to the limited range of human forearm's motion, the robot could not continuously rotate the valve, hindering its application in industry. In this work, we propose an approach to initiate continuous rotation when the forearm angle exceeds a threshold. This switch of control authority exemplifies the concept shared control from human-robot interaction, marking a further step in aerial teleoperation.

title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
comment: Accepted at IEEE Spoken Language Technology (SLT) 2026
summary: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.

title: Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Latency-Aware Multi-Agent Workflow Learning for Recurrent Queries
summary: Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-based MAS) have shown remarkable success in solving complex tasks by coordinating specialized agents through multi-step workflows. To overcome the high cost and specificity of manually designed workflows, recent research has shifted toward learning them automatically. However, a key limitation remains: while agent calls introduce significant latency due to model inference time and service congestion, most automated methods optimize solely for downstream performance, ignoring execution time (makespan). This issue is amplified when workflows are reused across recurring queries, making latency accumulate over time. This limits deployment in recurrent applications such as AI customer support and AI cloud troubleshooting, where users expect fast responses. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new problem, termed latency-aware workflow generation, where the objective is to minimize workflow makespan while aiming to retain downstream performance. We propose LAWA (Latency-Aware Workflow optimizAtion), a novel framework that reduces makespan via theoretically grounded graph edits targeting critical-path bottlenecks. By unifying a graph generator with this graph-editing procedure, LAWA supports both de novo workflow generation and refinement of existing ones. Empirical results across seven benchmarks demonstrate that LAWA significantly reduces makespan while achieving competitive task performance, supporting efficient reuse of multi-agent workflows for recurrent queries.

title: From Field to Planning: Learning Temporal Polar Gradient Fields for Vision-based AAV Trajectory Planning in Dynamic Environments
summary: Autonomous Aerial Vehicle (AAV) trajectory planning requires real-time and accurate safety gradient guidance, especially in dynamic environments. Existing methods typically rely on static maps and dynamic obstacle tracking to construct gradient fields, imposing heavy computational burdens and yielding conservative trajectories. To address these limitations, we propose a two-stage Field-to-Planning (F2P) learning framework to provide accurate and efficient safety gradients for trajectory planning in dynamic environments. In the first stage, we introduce an Ego-centric Polar Occupancy (EPO) representation that naturally matches the geometry of the onboard camera frustum, while supporting unstructured scene modeling. Subsequently, we formulate a Temporal Polar Gradient Field (TPGF) via multi-kernel separable Gaussian convolution to provide unified safety gradients, without explicitly distinguishing between static and dynamic obstacles. To mitigate the inherent spatial ambiguity introduced by applying convolutions within the polar grid, we propose an ESDF-guided offline learning strategy that incorporates geometric priors into TPGF. In the second stage, we employ the calibrated TPGF to guide the trajectory planning policy in a self-supervised learning manner. Comparative results with other approaches demonstrate the superiority of our method. Extensive real-world experiments within various cluttered dynamic environments validate the real-time performance and robustness on resource-constrained onboard systems.

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
summary:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects.
  In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
summary: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.

title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/dcommey/ztac
summary: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.

title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
summary: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

title: Multi-modal Representation Fusion for Long-term Microsurgical Anastomosis Trajectory Anticipation
summary: Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations. Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis. However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions. In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network. Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization. A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.

title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
summary:
Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships.
  We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks.
  GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Code, rules, lessons, data and evolve reports: https://github.com/agentic-loops-x/Reels-RSI
summary: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

title: DSR-Net: Learning Dynamic Skeletal Relations for 3D Human Pose Estimation
summary: 3D human pose estimation requires accurate modeling of motion-dependent skeletal structures and inter-joint dependencies. Existing methods typically rely on fixed skeletal topologies in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) or implicitly capture joint relations through attention mechanisms, limiting their adaptability to diverse motion patterns. To address this issue,we proposeDSR-Net, a dynamic structural representation learning framework for 3D human pose estimation. Specifically, a Dynamic Skeletal Relation (DSR) module is introduced to learn adaptive inter-joint dependencies beyond predefined skeletal connections. Based on the learned relations, a hierarchical relation-aware fusion strategy is developed to facilitate effective interaction between structural and temporal representations. In addition, a lightweight Residual Skeletal Recalibration Module (RSRM) is designed to enhance the stability of structure-aware features with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP demonstrate that DSR-Net achieves MPJPEs of 37.9 mm and 14.9 mm, respectively, consistently improving over strong baselines. The results validate the effectiveness of dynamic skeletal relation modeling for robust 3D human pose estimation.

title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
summary: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.

title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
summary: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.

title: PAG-Agent: Zero-Shot Personalized Music Album Generation via Aesthetic Profile Distillation
summary: Large Music Models (LMMs) can synthesize high-fidelity audio and support increasingly flexible prompt control, yet modeling the subjective preferences of an individual listener remains underexplored. We present PAG-Agent, a zero-shot multimodal framework that uses an explicit Personal Aesthetic Profile to bridge user preference inference and music generation control. A multimodal LLM distills favorite-song audio and contextual user information into this structured representation, which a planning LLM translates into generation instructions for existing music synthesizers. We further introduce PA-Eval, which evaluates personalization through the Aesthetic Consistency Score (ACS) for target-user alignment and the Aesthetic Specificity Index (ASI) for cross-user specificity. Experiments with Personal-100 on multiple MLLM and music-generation backbones show consistent improvements over generic and direct conditioning. A 50-participant follow-up study further shows a correlation $r=0.64$ between ACS and subjective preference.

title: EVISTA: Unified Multimodal Video Search with Evidence-Aware Temporal Path Optimization
summary: In the era of big data, precise event retrieval from large video collections has become increasingly important and challenging. In particular, locating multiple events from the same video in their temporal order is difficult when different events are described by different types of evidence, such as visual content, on-screen text, and spoken words. We develop EVISTA, a unified multimodal video retrieval system for the Ho Chi Minh City AI Challenge 2026, which integrates visual-semantic, OCR, ASR, object, and metadata search over a shared keyframe index, and propose TEMPO-P, an evidence-aware temporal path optimization method for ordered multi-event retrieval. Building EVISTA for this task reveals two limitations of independent event retrieval: a relevant video may be missed when one event is weakly retrieved, and independently retrieved event candidates may be temporally inconsistent or unable to represent events defined primarily by text or speech.
